claims.text: Low-level doping of transition-metal nanoparticles shifts the d-band center.
Shifting the d-band center directly modulates the binding strength of key reaction intermediates.
Changes in intermediate binding strength tune catalytic activity and selectivity.
A second transition-metal dopant can shift the d-band center without altering nanoparticle size, morphology, support interactions, defects, or other physical structure.
The d-band center position of surface atoms is the structural or electronic mediator governing the proposed catalytic changes.
Dopant-induced tuning of the d-band center alters the catalyst's electronic structure.
The altered electronic structure changes adsorption energies of key reaction intermediates.
Changes in adsorption energies lead to changes in catalytic activity and selectivity.
An optimally shifted d-band center will systematically enhance catalytic activity and/or selectivity relative to an otherwise matched monometallic baseline.
The predicted performance enhancement will be accompanied by changes in adsorption energies and reaction kinetics.
The proposed relationship should hold only over a defined range of temperatures, pressures, and low dopant concentrations that do not cause structural or defect changes.
Prior trends suggest a correlation between d-band-center position and catalytic performance.
Undetected morphological or defect-related effects may contribute to the observed activity changes.
Comparing a monometallic control with a low-dopant series while matching particle size, morphology, and support can test whether d-band shifts correlate with adsorption and catalytic performance.
The absence of a systematic correlation among d-band-center shifts, adsorption energies, and activity or selectivity relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
